speakerTitle: Consultant in Acute Medicine & Infectious Diseases
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Assessment & Infection Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician and infection specialist who chairs the antimicrobial stewardship round and teaches trainees to reason from source to organism to drug to source control.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Three patients arrive in the same hour, all "septic." A 78-year-old man with a cough and a lactate of 4. A 55-year-old woman with loin pain, rigors, and a blocked ureteric stent. A 34-year-old with a red, agonising, rapidly spreading leg and a temperature of 39.5°C. All three get the sepsis bundle — but the antibiotic, the imaging, and the knife they need are completely different. "Broad-spectrum and fluids" is where sepsis management starts, not where it ends. Tonight we go source by source, because the source dictates the drug and decides whether the patient needs a surgeon tonight.

1 · 🧭 The organising principle — find the source, control the source

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign gives you the resuscitation frame (cultures, lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for shock, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors for MAP ≥65). But two questions decide the case beyond the bundle:

  1. What is the likely source, and therefore the likely bug? — this chooses the antibiotic.
  2. Does the source need a physical intervention? — drainage, decompression, or debridement. Antibiotics cannot sterilise pus, an obstructed system, or dead tissue.
Antibiotics treat the blood; source control treats the sepsis. An undrained abscess laughs at meropenem.
⚠️ Source control is a resuscitation, not a "when-stable" luxury

SSC 2021: achieve source control as soon as logistically feasible — for obstructed urosepsis, necrotising fasciitis, and undrained collections that is measured in hours, not the next elective list. Delayed source control is one of the commonest reversible causes of refractory septic shock. The patient may need to go to theatre before they look fully resuscitated.

2 · 🦠 The master table — syndrome → bugs → empiric therapy → source control

Necrotising fasciitisGroup A Strep, S. aureus, or polymicrobial (incl. anaerobes/Gram-negatives)Carbapenem/pip-tazo + clindamycin + vancomycinUrgent surgical debridement (SURGICAL EMERGENCY)

3 · 🫁 Pneumonia — CURB-65 and the pathogen map

CURB-65 stratifies community-acquired pneumonia severity and site of care — one point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60), and age ≥65.

ScoreMortality riskDisposition
0–1Low (<3%)Consider home, oral antibiotics
2Intermediate (~9%)Hospital admission
3–5High (15–40%)Assess for ICU/HDU

Distinguish CAP (Strep pneumoniae dominant; Legionella and atypicals in the severe/at-risk) from HAP/VAP (≥48 h in hospital — Pseudomonas, Enterobacterales, MRSA drive empiric choice). Cover MRSA and Pseudomonas empirically only when risk factors are present (prior isolation, structural lung disease, recent IV antibiotics). Send a Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen in severe CAP.

💡 The effusion you must not miss

Any pneumonia with a pleural effusion needs a diagnostic tap. A pH <7.2, low glucose, high LDH, or frank pus means empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion — that is source control, and it needs a chest drain, not just more antibiotics.

4 · 🫘 Urosepsis — obstruction is the emergency

Pyelonephritis is common and usually responds to antibiotics. But an obstructed, infected urinary system (pyonephrosis) is a surgical/urological emergency — pus under pressure above a stone or blocked stent will not clear with any antibiotic and drives fulminant shock.

Fever + obstruction = drainage tonight. The kidney above a stone is an abscess with a ureter.

Image early with CT KUB or ultrasound. Relieve obstruction urgently with a percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent. Antibiotics (ceftriaxone or pip-tazobactam; carbapenem if ESBL risk) buy time but do not substitute for decompression. Remember Enterococcus in healthcare-associated and catheter-related urosepsis.

5 · 🩻 Intra-abdominal sepsis — drain it, then keep it short

Perforation, abscess, cholangitis, and ischaemic bowel need source control (percutaneous drainage or surgery) plus cover for Enterobacterales and anaerobes (pip-tazobactam, or ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or a carbapenem). For cholangitis, biliary decompression (ERCP) is the source control.

🎯 STOP-IT — shorter is enough

The STOP-IT trial showed that after adequate source control of a complicated intra-abdominal infection, a fixed short course (~4 days) of antibiotics was as effective as a longer course guided by clinical resolution. Once the pus is drained, you do not need two weeks of antibiotics — the drain did the work.

6 · 🔥 Skin & soft tissue — the leg you must not miss

Cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis (spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness) — treat with flucloxacillin (or co-amoxiclav), mark the border, and review. Most "bilateral cellulitis" is actually venous stasis/eczema — reserve antibiotics for genuine infection.

⚠️ Necrotising fasciitis — the surgical emergency hiding as cellulitis

Red flags: pain out of proportion to the visible skin, rapid progression (marked in hours), systemic toxicity, skin anaesthesia, crepitus, bullae, or dusky/necrotic skin. The LRINEC score can support suspicion but a normal score never excludes it — this is a clinical diagnosis confirmed in theatre. Management is immediate surgical exploration and debridement (the imaging is the operation), broad-spectrum antibiotics, and clindamycin to switch off toxin/exotoxin production (the Eagle effect — it works independent of bacterial growth phase, unlike β-lactams). Add IVIG in streptococcal toxic shock. Delay measured in hours costs limbs and lives.

7 · 🧠 Meningitis & encephalitis — the clock is antibiotics, not the CT

Suspected bacterial meningitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness ± non-blanching rash) is a time-critical emergency.

Do not delay antibiotics for the LP or the CT. Blood cultures, then ceftriaxone — within the hour.
  • Antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2 g IV (BD); add amoxicillin to cover Listeria in those >50 or immunocompromised.
  • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just before the first antibiotic dose — reduces neurological sequelae/hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans trial).
  • Aciclovir if encephalitis features (personality change, seizures, focal signs, dysphasia) to cover HSV — do not wait for the PCR.
  • LP timing: do it promptly, but a CT first is needed if reduced/fluctuating GCS, focal neurology, papilloedema, seizures, or immunocompromise — and give antibiotics before the CT/LP if any delay. Check clotting/platelets.

8 · 🩹 Catheter-related bloodstream infection

Suspect CRBSI in any patient with a central line and unexplained sepsis, especially with erythema at the exit site or bacteraemia with coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, or Candida. The diagnostic gem:

💡 Differential time-to-positivity

Blood drawn from the line turns positive ≥2 hours before a simultaneous peripheral culture → the line is the source. Take paired cultures (line + peripheral) before antibiotics.

Source control = remove the line for S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, tunnel infection, septic shock, or persistent bacteraemia. Empiric cover: vancomycin (Gram-positives/MRSA) + anti-pseudomonal Gram-negative cover; add an echinocandin if candidaemia is suspected. Antibiotic "lock" therapy only in selected salvage situations.

9 · ❤️ Infective endocarditis — the modified Duke criteria in brief

Suspect IE with fever plus a new murmur, embolic phenomena, or persistent bacteraemia with a typical organism. Diagnosis uses the modified Duke criteria: major = typical organism in persistently positive blood cultures + echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new valve regurgitation); minor = predisposing heart condition/IVDU, fever ≥38°C, vascular phenomena (Janeway lesions, emboli), immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis), and suggestive microbiology. Definite IE = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor. Take 3 sets of blood cultures from different sites before antibiotics, get a TOE, and refer to the endocarditis MDT. Surgery for heart failure, perivalvular abscess, large mobile vegetations, or uncontrolled/resistant infection.

☠️ M&M — the "cellulitis" that was eating the leg

A 34-year-old man was admitted with a red, swollen, exquisitely painful lower leg and started on IV flucloxacillin for "cellulitis." Overnight he needed escalating opioids — the pain was wildly out of proportion to a leg that looked only moderately red, and the ward attributed his tachycardia and confusion to "sepsis responding slowly." At the morning round the erythema had climbed 15 cm, the skin was dusky with a bulla, and one patch was numb. He had necrotising fasciitis from Group A Streptococcus. He went to theatre 14 hours after arrival — by then he needed extensive debridement and an ICU admission with streptococcal toxic shock, and lost much of the calf musculature. Lessons: pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, and skin anaesthesia are necrotising fasciitis until a surgeon says otherwise; the diagnosis is made in theatre, not on a normal LRINEC score or an X-ray; and clindamycin must be added to shut down toxin production. Every hour of antibiotics-only was an hour the infection kept dissecting the fascial plane.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. The source dictates the drug and decides the surgeon — "broad-spectrum and fluids" is the start, not the plan.
  2. Source control is resuscitation: obstruction, necrotising infection, and undrained pus need intervention in hours.
  3. CURB-65 guides pneumonia disposition; tap and drain any complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema.
  4. Obstructed urosepsis = emergency decompression (nephrostomy/stent) — antibiotics alone will not save it.
  5. After adequate source control of intra-abdominal sepsis, keep antibiotics short (~4 days, STOP-IT).
  6. Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical, theatre-confirmed emergency — add clindamycin for toxin; a normal LRINEC never excludes it.
  7. Never delay antibiotics ± aciclovir ± dexamethasone for the LP/CT in suspected meningitis/encephalitis.
  8. CRBSI: paired cultures, differential time-to-positivity, and remove the line for S. aureus/Candida/shock.
  9. Endocarditis: 3 sets of cultures, echo, modified Duke criteria, MDT.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with pyelonephritis, rigors and a lactate of 4 has a 9 mm stone obstructing the ureter. What is the priority?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Emergency decompression of the obstructed, infected system — this is source control and it takes priority over everything except immediate resuscitation. An obstructed infected kidney (pyonephrosis) is essentially a walled abscess under pressure; no antibiotic will sterilise pus behind a blocked ureter, and delay drives refractory septic shock. I would give IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone or pip-tazobactam; carbapenem if ESBL risk) and fluids while arranging urgent urological drainage — a percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent the same night, not on the next elective list. Source control here is measured in hours.

moderatorQs.q: Why does clindamycin belong in the necrotising fasciitis regimen, and what confirms the diagnosis?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Clindamycin is added because it is a protein-synthesis inhibitor that switches off bacterial exotoxin and M-protein production — including streptococcal superantigens driving toxic shock — and it works independent of bacterial growth phase (the Eagle effect), unlike β-lactams which fail against a large, slow-growing inoculum. So the regimen is a broad-spectrum agent (carbapenem or pip-tazobactam) + vancomycin + clindamycin, ± IVIG in strep toxic shock. The diagnosis is confirmed surgically — the operation is both the diagnostic test and the treatment. Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, skin anaesthesia, crepitus and bullae are the clues; a normal LRINEC score does not exclude it, so clinical suspicion mandates immediate surgical exploration.

moderatorQs.q: How do you sequence antibiotics, dexamethasone, aciclovir, LP and CT in suspected meningitis?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The overriding rule is that antibiotics must not be delayed by imaging or the LP. Take blood cultures, then give ceftriaxone 2 g IV (add amoxicillin for Listeria if >50 or immunocompromised) with dexamethasone 10 mg IV just before or with the first dose (reduces sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis). Add aciclovir if there are encephalitis features to cover HSV. Do the LP promptly, but perform a CT head first if there is reduced/fluctuating consciousness, focal neurology, papilloedema, seizures, or immunocompromise — and in that case the antibiotics have already gone in. Check clotting and platelets before the LP.

audienceQs.q: How does CURB-65 change what I do for a pneumonia patient?
audienceQs.answerHTML: CURB-65 scores one point each for Confusion, Urea >7, Respiratory rate ≥30, low Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60), and age ≥65. A score of 0–1 is low mortality and often suitable for home with oral antibiotics; 2 warrants admission; 3–5 is high mortality and should prompt ICU/HDU assessment. In severe CAP add a macrolide for atypical/Legionella cover, send Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens, and always look for a parapneumonic effusion to tap — a pH <7.2 or pus means empyema needing a chest drain, which no oral antibiotic will fix.

audienceQs.q: After we drain an intra-abdominal abscess, how long should antibiotics run?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Short — provided source control was adequate. The STOP-IT trial showed that after adequate drainage or surgical control of a complicated intra-abdominal infection, a fixed ~4-day course gave equivalent outcomes to a longer, symptom-guided course. So once the collection is drained and the patient is improving, plan around 4 days rather than defaulting to 7–14. Empiric cover targets Enterobacterales and anaerobes (pip-tazobactam, or ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or a carbapenem), de-escalated on cultures. If source control was incomplete or there is ongoing collection, the clock resets — the short course assumes the pus is actually gone.

audienceQs.q: How do we prove a central line is the source of the sepsis before pulling it?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Take paired blood cultures — one from the central line and one from a peripheral vein — at the same time and before antibiotics. If the sample from the line flags positive at least 2 hours earlier than the peripheral one (differential time-to-positivity), that points to the line as the source. Typical organisms are coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas and other Gram-negatives. The line should be removed (not just treated through) for S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, a tunnel/exit-site infection, septic shock, or persistent bacteraemia — empiric cover is vancomycin plus anti-pseudomonal Gram-negative cover, adding an echinocandin if candidaemia is likely.
